title: Cicli Pucci Custom Painted Ron’s Bikes for Blue Lug : A Globetrotting Collaboration – Jonny Pucci
content:
For a special run of Ron’s Bikes Blue Lug edition frames, the Japanese retailer pinged painter and artist Jonny Pucci to create bikes unlike anything the brand has sold before…

Wedged between Tucson, Arizona, and Nogales, Mexico, is a land seemingly purpose-built for wandering and reflection. Where desert plants intermingle with rolling grasslands that suddenly give way to isolated mountains, rising dramatically to create biologically distinct islands in the sky. This desert landscape near Arizona’s southern border feels like a kind of balm for the soul, and with an endless patchwork of varying gravel roads and single-track paths, a cyclist can push their body to the limit while their spirit has a day at the spa. It’s a place to ride, camp, and connect with friends and the natural world.

For many years now I’ve been returning to this corner of country as a sort of spiritual respite. This past winter, on one of my annual pilgrimages, I met up with a few dear friends, including gravel aficionado and connoisseur of quaintness, Ronnie Romance. Ron introduced me to this area years ago, and since then he’s rarely missed a season, stating adamantly that aside from his home state of Connecticut, Arizona is the most beautiful place in the lower 48. After each day’s ride filled with desert bathing and noteworthy local pizza, our small group was treated to a sensory experience of light and color. As the sun made its retreat, the western sky became a furnace of orange and yellow hues, while to the east, a full moon rose and hung balanced between the creeping blue of night and the evaporating violet of the lower atmosphere. Sitting in awe, our campfire would slowly take over each night as the dominant source of light.

On one evening, as darkness closed in around us, I posited to the group that I had found myself at a crossroads in my career painting high-end and custom bicycles. I was balancing painting bikes with my life as a mural painter and artist, and after almost a decade and a half of painting alongside the legendary Joe Bell of JB Paint, I thought that rather than a perpetual stream of bikes needing my constant time and attention, I wanted to find a way to dovetail my two careers into one.

I imagined a scenario where I could be a sort of traveling tailor of bikes, bringing my specific skills and passed-down knowledge to different locations to share with other painters, taking part in limited and unique projects that could benefit from my personal Cicli Pucci touch. In response, Ronnie submitted, “I have a batch of Alumax II and CR1 Country Road frames being constructed back home for Blue Lug Bicycle Shop in Japan. Why don’t you go to Tokyo and paint those? They’re being shipped unpainted…”

A little over a year before all of this, I took on a solo bike tour across Japan which started in Tokyo. I didn’t have a hard plan at the time for where the tour would go, but I knew that when I arrived, my first stop would have to be at Blue Lug Bike Shop. At this point, Blue Lug should need no introduction; celebrated around the world, the good folks at Blue Lug are known for creating one-of-a-kind rides that are both meticulously intentional and effortlessly cool. And as the premier importer of Riv bikes in Japan, they were already familiar with my work at JB’s for Rivendell.

In those first few days, the friends I made at Blue Lug gave me advice on where to eat, what to see, and what routes to explore on my tour. Their staff manager, Wentz, brought me behind the mechanics counter, where I met fellow in-house custom bike painter Konno-Boy, aka Cook Paintworks. While my lack of Japanese and Konno’s limited English would seem a hindrance, our common language of paint and design made communication a certainty, and a fast friendship was made. On my journey across the country, Konno, Wentz, and others checked in on my progress, gave travel and cultural advice, and even bailed me out when I broke down and needed a critical component mailed to me on short notice.

After nearly 1,200 km of riding, I returned to Tokyo for a final night of dinner and drinks before returning home to San Diego, CA. Over rice bowls and sake flights, my new friends and I cracked jokes, talked shop, and teased plans for a future collaboration between Blue Lug, the Cook, and myself. Surely one was coming; we just had to wait for the right opportunity.

After Arizona, I started to draft a plan that would take me back to the land of the rising sun. With some 30 frames being shipped to Blue Lug, the exact number of bikes that would receive our limited edition paint was to be determined, as was their arrival date sometime in May or possibly even June. For design inspiration, Ron nudged me towards the Klein bikes of the early 90’s. Different paint styles come in and out of vogue, but a good fade can be timeless when executed correctly.

The Klein Attitude, with its linear fade paint scheme, was a childhood dream machine of Ron’s that oozes cool even today, and the Alumax II’s construction at the hands of legendary MTB innovator and fabricator Frank the Welder would give credence to the frame’s ’90s pedigree. Fat aluminum tubes lend themselves to this sort of tight fading, but for the more svelte and skinny steel Country Road bikes built by Darren Larkin, I suggested a more gradual top-to-bottom approach, without any breaks between where one color stops and the other begins. As for color choice, I didn’t have to look any further than our shared experience of those panoramic sunsets in the Arizona desert.

Traditional Japanese Ukiyo-e woodblock printing employs gradients as a way to convey the color relationships of the natural world. By blending one color into the next, artists showcase how light at a certain hour can create color combinations that are timeless, as they are based in reality. With this in mind, it only seemed natural that our color choices should do the same, chasing a feeling rather than a trend. The warm setting sun and the cool transition of the rising moon would be my jumping-off point. With the wheels set in motion, there was nothing left to do but book travel across the Pacific, and hope the frames would arrive before I did.

When I finally touched down in Tokyo, I made my way back to Blue Lug Kamiuma, reuniting with Konno, Wentz, and the others. Konno brought me into his space and over the next few days I became acquainted with his shop layout and painting process. We began by looking over his catalog of premixed paint pigments and pearlescent colors, selecting what we would need to recreate the sunset fades of the desert night.

While I began to stir different paints and pearls, back in the US, a special edition run of color matching bags, caps, and bandanas was being put in the works by Ron for delivery to Japan. As Konno and I bumped and jostled around his Tokyo-sized workshop, we became accustomed to sharing the tight space. Breaking the job into pieces we could tackle individually, we both reveled in the chance to work as a painting team instead of our usual solo acts, sharing in the highs and lows of the unforgiving process that is painting bicycle frames.

Any painter with a decent amount of experience in this industry will have the same stories to tell of all the ways that a job can go sideways. As the saying goes, we all make mistakes, but a good painter is the one who can fix theirs without anyone noticing. The primer paint gets contaminated; back to the kitchen. You accidentally sand through the clear coat and into the color; back to the kitchen. Your vinyl cutter malfunctions; oh f*ck. Konno and I had experienced all these issues alone, and now we were finding ways to tackle them together.

Over the next month, I settled into my residency with the crew at Blue Lug Kamiuma. My new coworkers and I exchanged techniques and gave each other lessons in foreign languages. I learned the subtle nuance between politely thanking someone for their hard work by saying “Otsukaresamadesu” and the more casual “Otsssss,” and passed on new lingual terms like “bitchin’” and “chingadera.” As the frames arrived and the work began, it was decided that only four Alumax II’s and four CR-1’s would be dressed in our limited release colorway. Since I only mixed a small pint of each paint by feel instead of using a color code, the specific hues used in this collaboration would be nearly impossible to replicate, making them truly limited.

By bringing these unique bikes to life, along with their matching softgoods, myself, Ronnie, Konno, and Blue Lug managed to create something that feels like more than just a special bike brand collaboration. It was as much an expression of a shared experience in a place of deep importance for my buddy Ron and me, as it was the culmination of a plan made between new friends in a cozy izakaya almost two years before.

As for me personally, my experience at Blue Lug was an opportunity to step towards the artistic goals I had set out to achieve in the first place. A blueprint for how to produce uncompromisingly top-quality work in a space that was as inconvenient as it was unfamiliar. For a lucky few, it will be a chance to own and enjoy a bespoke machine that carries all of these shared experiences down whatever road may come.

Huge thanks to Blue Lug, Ron’s Bikes, and Jonny Pucci for this one!
